sentences.text: 1 This claim petition is filed under section 166 of the M.V. Act, seeking compensation for the injuries sustained in a road traffic accident.
2. Brief case of the petitioner in the nutshell:

It is the case of the petitioner that, on ill fated day i.e.., 25.07.2016 at about 4.30 p.m,
the petitioner was traveling in the car bearing Reg.No.KA-53-C-2378 along with Smt.
Naznee Khanam and the driver of the car proceeding from K.R.Puram to Addagal village, when came near Kodicharuvu gate, Srinivasapura Taluk, Kolar, the driver of the car drove it in a rash & negligent manner, and in order to avoid the opposite coming motorcycle, suddenly applied the brakes, due to which the said car toppled and dashed to the road side tree and caused accident.
As a result of impact, inmates of the car had sustained grievous injuries.

It is further urged that, the petitioner was shifted to R.L. Jalappa Hospital, Kolar and then he was shifted to KIMS Hospital, and he was treated as inpatient and he had spent substantial amount towards medical expenses.

It is urged that, before the accident he was hale and healthy and was doing business and was earning Rs.20,000/- p.m., and due to the accidental injuries he was unable to work as such he suffered both financially and emotionally.

Further contended that the accident happened because of rash and negligent of the car driver as such the respondents are jointly and severally liable to pay compensation and prayed to grant a compensation amount.
3. Prior to remand, notice was duly served to respondent No.1, the respondent No.1 did not appear before this Tribunal.
Hence he was placed exparte.

4. Prior to remand, after service of notice respondent No.2 spurred in rush to the Court by filing written statement rather objections to the main petition contending that the petition itself is not maintainable either law or on facts.
The respondent No.2 admitting the issuance of insurance policy in respect of vehicle bearing Reg.No.KA-53-C-2378.
However the liability if any is pleaded to be subject to the terms & conditions of the policy.
Non - compliance of section's 147, 149(2) of MV Act is pleaded.
It is also urged that there is inordinate delay of 25 days that itself vibrantly discloses that the case is foisted so as to wangle the compensation amount from the insurance company.

Without prejudice to the said contention it is averred that the driver of the car did not possess valid &
effective DL as on the date of accident.
Despite knowing the said fact the owner thereof had handed over its possession to such a driver.
On account of willful breach of the terms & conditions of the policy by the insured, the insurance company is not liable to indemnify him.
Further denied all the allegation made in the petition.
Hence prayed to dismiss the petition.

Aggrieved by it, the petitioner herein preferred an appeal (for modify the judgment and award passed by this Tribunal) before the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in MFA No.5012/2018 (M.V) which was allowed.

Consequently, the judgment & award passed by this Tribunal on 14.02.2018 was partly set-side and the case was remanded to the tribunal in respect of assessment of disability and quantum of compensation is concerned and to reconsider the matter afresh after Saddam Baig vs Srinivas G N on 16 February, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/186331580/

sentences.text: As already held herein above, the petitioner proved that he has sustained injuries in RTA which is caused by the vehicle belonging to respondent No.1 and insured with the respondent no.2.
Hence the petitioner is entitle for compensation.
This Court has already held Issue No.1 in the affirmative which makes it more than obvious that the petitioner is entitled for compensation.

Needless to state the quantum of compensation which is awarded has to be proportionate to the nature of the injuries and the compensation has to be awarded by keeping in mind the pecuniary damages and non-pecuniary damages suffered by the injured-claimant.
By pecuniary damages this Court is referring to the actual loss sustained by the petitioner, which can be determined in terms of money, by taking into account the oral or documentary evidence.

Whereas for non-pecuniary damages this Court is referring to the losses that the claimant has though suffered, but will not be able to prove for the reason that it can neither be calculated in terms of the money nor can it be proved leading documentary evidence.
Perhaps the non-pecuniary damages can be figured out by looking into the facts of each case by taking into account the nature of injuries and the aftermath.

It is required to be reminded to oneself that compensation in a case arising out of injury can never be granted on mathematical precision and invariably a good amount of guesswork is involved while determining the compensation in such cases.
13.

Perhaps unlike in a fatal case, in a case involving bodily injury the victim is left to suffer throughout his life; and hence it becomes the bounden duty of the tribunal to award compensation to a victim of permanent disability so as to bring in sustainability and also to ensure that victim is not pushed to poverty.

Be that as it may the law well settled itself that it is an impact of physical disability on particular avocation which is relevant for the purpose of assessment of compensation under the loss of future income as held by the Hon'ble Apex Court in (2011) 1 SCC 343 in the case of Rajkumar V/s. Ajaykumar and another, wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court held as follows;
Therefore, the Tribunal has to first decide whether there is any permanent disability and if so the extent of such permanent disability.

This means that the tribunal should consider and decide with reference to the evidence:
(i) whether the disablement is permanent or temporary;
(ii) if the disablement is permanent, whether it is permanent total disablement or permanent partial disablement,
(iii) if the disablement percentage is expressed with reference to any specific limb,
then the effect of such disablement of the limb on the functioning of the entire body,
that is the permanent disability suffered by the person.
If the Tribunal concludes that there is no permanent disability then there is no question of proceeding further and determining the loss of future earning capacity.
But if the Tribunal concludes that there is permanent disability then it will proceed to ascertain its extent.

After the Tribunal ascertains the actual extent of permanent disability of the claimant based on the medical evidence, it has to determine whether such permanent disability has affected or will affect his earning capacity.

sentences.text: Ascertainment of the effect of the permanent disability on the actual earning capacity involves three steps.

The Tribunal has to first ascertain what activities the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of the permanent ability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The second step is to ascertain his avocation, profession and nature of work before the accident, as also his age.

The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood, or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions, but could carry on some other or lesser scale of activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood.
For example, if the left hand of a claimant is amputated, the permanent physical or functional disablement may be assessed around 60%.
If the claimant was a driver or a carpenter, the actual loss of earning capacity may virtually be hundred percent, if he is neither able to drive or do carpentry.

On the other hand, if the claimant was a clerk in government service, the loss of his left hand may not result in loss of employment and he may still be continued as a clerk as he could perform his clerical functions; and in that event the loss of earning capacity will not be 100% as in the case of a driver or carpenter, nor 60% which is the actual physical disability, but far less.

In fact, there may not be any need to award any compensation under the head of `loss of future earnings', if the claimant continues in government service, though he may be awarded compensation under the head of loss of amenities as a consequence of losing his hand.

Sometimes the injured claimant may be continued in service, but may not found suitable for discharging the duties attached to the post or job which he was earlier holding, on account of his disability, and may therefore be shifted to some other suitable but lesser post with lesser emoluments, in which case there should be a limited award under the head of loss of future earning capacity, taking note of the reduced earning capacity.

sentences.text: The respondent had got summoned the official of Insurance Department and he has produced the IT returns of the petitioner for the year 2019-20 and 2020-2021.
On careful perusal of IT returns which is also appended with ITR-4 sugam it reflects that the income of the petitioner for the year 2019-20 is Rs.3,06,880/-.
On careful perusal of the said documents it reflects the business code as 090003 / sale of motor parts and accessories whole sale and retail.
Which means to say the petitioner has continued his business.
Added more the respondent has also got summoned Income Tax returns for the year 2020-21 wherein also the total income is shown to the tune of Rs.3,74,802/-.
On careful perusal of documents it reflects that the petitioner was doing the business of goods carriage.

The learned counsel for the petitioner argued stoutly by filing additional affidavit of the petitioner stating that, after the accident the petitioner was not in a position to do any work and he was under treatment of physiotherapy and PW.1 has deposed that he not aware of the IT returns produced by respondent No.2 and he has not filed any Income Tax returns for the year 2019- 2020 and 2020-2021.
It is relevant to note that PW.1 himself had categorically admitted during the course of cross examination that, the PAN number, name and address mentioned in Ex.P.19 IT returns is correct.
Ex.P.19 IT returns is also akin to Ex.R.2 IT returns.
Much was canvassed by learned counsel for the petitioner contending that, the petitioner has not at all filed IT returns for the year 2019-20, 2020-21.
It is not out of context to observe that, now the IT returns will be filed based on Aadhar OTP verification and same is ascertained while cross examination of RW2.
Only after the authentication of Aadhar through OTP the IT returns of the petitioner will be filed.
When such being the case the contention urged by the petitioner that he is totally unaware of the IT returns of the year 2019-2020, 2020-2021 is not at all believable in the eye of law.
At the same juncture this court has to consider that for the year 2017-18 and 2018-19 the petitioner has not at all filed any IT returns which means to say he has not having any income what so ever.
Further more as per the documentary proof summoned by respondent themselves the petitioner has not at filed IT after 2021 which means to say the petitioner is not having any income after that year.

The evidence of doctor discloses that the petitioner is not in a position to walk because of paraplegia.

The petitioner can continue his business by sitting in office with some difficulty.

Considering the nature of injuries, line of treatment and on appreciation of the clinical findings noted by the doctor, the possibility of the fact that the petitioner may be having economical or functional disability to the extent of 60%, cannot be ruled out.
Therefore, this Tribunal consider the functional disability of the petitioner at 60%.

sentences.text: The petitioner has relied upon wound certificate, Discharge Summaries, progress reports, lab reports and X-ray films in order to show that he had sustained injuries and underwent pain and sufferings.
The Ex.P- 6, 8, 9, 15, 29 to 32 reveal that the petitioner has indeed suffered the injuries contended by him in the petition.
The petitioner at this young age has suffered a lot because of this ill fated accident.

Considering the nature of the injuries mentioned in wound certificate and in treatment certificate, it can be said that the petitioner must have underwent enormous amount of physical pain and sufferings, for which, an amount of .1,00,000/- can be held to be just and proper compensation under this head.
(B) TOWARDS MEDICAL EXPENSES:

The petitioner has contended that he has spent more than .1,18,287.21 and Rs.81,158/- for his treatment and has produced medical bills prescriptions and receipts for having purchased materials as prescribed by the doctor which are marked as Ex.P-12, 13, 21 and 22 of which the total amount of medical expenses are .1,99,445/-.

There is no serious dispute regarding the medical bills produced and got marked by the petitioner and perusal of the said medical records especially the discharge summaries, medical bills and medical records/ certificates, makes it clear that the petitioner has incurred the medical expenses towards his treatment.
The total of medical bills is .1,99,445/- hence the medical expenses can be rounded off to .2,00,000/-.

Accordingly, the petitioner is entitled for an amount of .2,00,000/-
towards medical expenses.
(C) TOWARDS DIET, FOOD CHARGES:

As already observed the Ex.P-6, 8 and 9, make it amply clear that the petitioner underwent treatment at KIMS and NIMHANS Hospital, Bengaluru as an inpatient for a period of 99 days and the same is supported by depositions of PW.1 & 3.
Further during the said period the petitioner might have taken assistance from others and taken diet food.

On consideration of the injuries sustained by the petitioner and period of stay in the hospital and also taking into account the fact that the petitioner is suffering from paraplegia, this Tribunal is of the opinion that it is just and proper to award an amount of . 75,000/- under this head.
(D) TOWARDS NOURISHMENT AND CONVEYANCE CHARGES:
It is clear that the petitioner has suffered paraplegia and has lost sensation in both his lower limbs, which makes it obvious that he would need the assistance of an entire through out his life.

He stated that as per the advice of the doctors till today he has visited the KIMS hospital for 25 times in a car by paying Rs.1,000/- and per trip and visited NIMHANS Hospital for 10 times in a car by paying Rs.1,500/- per trip and also visited to Sri Rama Hospital, for 30 times in a auto by paying Rs.100/-

As it is clear that he is need and availed the services to visit the hospitals in frequently in such vehicles.

As such this court is of the opinion that the claimant is entitled for 'Nourishment and conveyance Charges'.
Therefore, it is just and reasonable to award .1,00,000/- towards Nourishment and conveyance charges.
(E) TOWARDS LOSS OF FUTURE EARNING CAPACITY ON ACCOUNT OF PERMANENT DISABILITY:
(i) The petitioner has alleged that due to injuries sustained in the accident, he has become permanently disabled and he is not in a position to work and earn his livelihood as he was doing earlier.
The factum of disability and loss of future earning is exhastively discussed above.
This tribunal after assessing the materials placed on record had held that the petitioner had suffered the 60% of disability.
It is clear that though the petitioner has not suffered any adverse effect on his mental faculty, but his physical condition is such that he needs assistance of some person to do his daily chores.
Further the assertion made by petitioner in his chief examination affidavit shows that he has lost sensation of both his lower limbs, but his upper limbs have not been affected due to the accident.

Hence taking in to consideration the nature of the injuries and also keeping in mind the fact that according to PW.3,
the petitioner has suffered paraplegia, this court holds that PW-1 has suffered 60 % whole body disability.
As such the disability is assessed at 60 %.
(ii) The PW-1 in his petition and also in his evidence has contended that as on the date of his examination before the court he was aged about 26 years.
Interestingly the PW-1 is an engineering graduate, the same is proved by Ex.P.14 Marks cards.

If the age of the petitioner as on the date of accident is 26 years., as per table given in Sarla Varma Vs.
Delhi Transport Corporation and another (2009 ACJ SC 1298), the multiplier would be '17'
(iii) The monthly income of the petitioner as noted above prior to the accident is Rs.24,070/-.

(F) ATTENDANT CHARGES:
It is clear that the petitioner has suffered paraplegia and has lost sensation in both his lower limbs, which makes it obvious that he would need the assistance of an entire through out his life.
As such this court is of the opinion that the claimant is entitled for 'Attendant Charges'.

Therefore, it is just and reasonable to award .50,000/-
towards attendant charges.
(G) LOSS OF INCOME DURING LAID-UP PERIOD:

Considering the nature of injuries, treatment given and the duration of his stay in the hospital, it is quite natural that petitioner was forced to remain absent from his work for a period of 6 months atleast.
Thus by taking into account the notional income of the petitioner, this Tribunal awards a sum of Rs.1,50,810/- (25,135 X 6) which is rounded off to Rs.1,51,000/- under this head.
(H) LOSS OF PROSPECTS OF MARRIAGE :
The petitioner had contended that due to the injuries sustained by him, he is unable to find a bride for marriage.
The evidence of doctor witness goes to show that the petitioner has paraplegia.
In fact there is a severe & permanent damage with little chance of any further meaningful recovery.
To put it in other words the chances of improvement in the condition of the petitioner are feeble.
In this view of the matter the petitioner is rendered permanently incapable of doing any work in future which would thus affect his future prospects both professionally and personally.
Obviously the matrimonial prospects of the victim/petitioner who suffered grievous accidental injuries, would also be severely affected.
To put it differently the marital prospects of the petitioner are bleak.
If a person chooses to be a bachelor throughout his life, it is his wish.
Whereas if a person is compelled to remain so because of an unfortunate accident then that will lead to mental agony.

In this regard the petitioner has relied on the decision of the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka reported in 2021 ACJ 2645 in the case of Divisional Manager, National Insurance, Company V/s Akash and another wherein it is held for loss of marriage prospects to the tune of Rs.5,00,000.

The Tribunal has to first ascertain what activities the claimant could carry on in spite of the permanent disability and what he could not do as a result of the permanent ability (this is also relevant for awarding compensation under the head of loss of amenities of life).
The third step is to find out whether (i) the claimant is totally disabled from earning any kind of livelihood, or (ii) whether in spite of the permanent disability, the claimant could still effectively carry on the activities and functions, which he was earlier carrying on, or (iii) whether he was prevented or restricted from discharging his previous activities and functions, but could carry on some other or lesser scale of activities and functions so that he continues to earn or can continue to earn his livelihood.

Perhaps unlike in a fatal case, in a case involving bodily injury the victim is left to suffer throughout his life; and hence it becomes the bounden duty of the tribunal to award compensation to a victim of permanent disability so as to bring in sustainability and also to ensure that victim is not pushed to poverty.
In order to prove the age of the petitioner, he has not produced any identity cards when such being the case this court has to dwell into the police documents coupled with medical records.
Be that as it may the law well settled itself that it is an impact of physical disability on particular avocation which is relevant for the purpose of assessment of compensation under the loss of future income as held by the Hon'ble Apex Court in (2011) 1 SCC 343 in the case of Rajkumar V/s. Ajaykumar and another, wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court held as follows;
Therefore, the Tribunal has to first decide whether there is any permanent disability and if so the extent of such permanent disability.
This means that the tribunal should consider and decide with reference to the evidence:
(i) whether the disablement is permanent or temporary;
(ii) if the disablement is permanent, whether it is permanent total disablement or permanent partial disablement,
(iii) if the disablement percentage is expressed with reference to any specific limb,
then the effect of such disablement of the limb on the functioning of the entire body,
that is the permanent disability suffered by the person.
If the Tribunal concludes that there is no permanent disability then there is no question of proceeding further and determining the loss of future earning capacity.
But if the Tribunal concludes that there is permanent disability then it will proceed to ascertain its extent.
After the Tribunal ascertains the actual extent of permanent disability of the claimant based on the medical evidence, it has to determine whether such permanent disability has affected or will affect his earning capacity.
